title: Build RAG Over Your PDFs, Part 1

scenes.text: Imagine asking questions to your insurance policy, or a 200 page textbook, and getting instant answers. [1] Over two episodes, we'll build exactly that, a RAG app over your own PDFs. [2] Part one, loading and storing the documents.

Here's the plan, from episode 32. [1] Load the PDF, and pull out its text. [2] Split the text into overlapping chunks. [3] Turn each chunk into an embedding. [4] Store everything in a vector database. [5] Next episode, we'll search it, and answer questions.

We need two free libraries. [1] pypdf, to read text from PDF files. [2] Chroma, a simple vector database, that also creates embeddings for us, automatically. [3] Install both with one command, pip install pypdf chromadb.

[1] Here's the code. [2] Import the two libraries. [3] Open the PDF, and join the text from every page. [4] Split it into words, and make chunks of 200 words, moving forward 150 at a time, so neighbouring chunks overlap by 50 words. [5] Create a Chroma database, saved in a folder, with a collection called docs. [6] Add all the chunks, each with an ID. Chroma embeds them for us. [7] Run it, and our PDF is stored, ready to search!

Why the overlap? [1] Without overlap, a key sentence can get cut in half, between two chunks, and neither chunk makes sense. [2] With overlap, the sentence appears whole in at least one chunk, so search can find it.

Here are four terms. [1] Ingestion, the process of loading, chunking, and storing documents. [2] Collection, a named group of chunks inside the database. [3] Persistent, saved to disk, so you only ingest once. [4] And ID, a unique label for every chunk, so we can cite it later.

Here's a common problem. [1] People expect every PDF to work. [2] Scanned PDFs are just pictures of pages, with no text inside. pypdf returns nothing. For those, you first need OCR, from use case 19, to read the text.

data.fact: Scanned PDFs are just images with no text. Run OCR first.
